etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First cited to 1694.
Ultimate derivation is unclear.
* One reference derives this from prefix あ (a, of uncertain meaning) + 諄い (kudoi, “repetitive, tedious, clunky, long-winded, insistent”).
*: However, there is no apparent fitting prefix, only 亜 (a-, “sub-, -ous, -ite”, most often found in chemistry or biology).
* Described in another source as deriving from 灰汁 (aku, “lye; harshness [as a characteristic of flavor or personality]”) + suffixing element どい (doi). This doi is probably from now-archaic adjective 利し・鋭し・疾し・敏し (toshi), modernized form とい (toi, “sharp, biting; fierce, vicious; fast, quick”).
Considering the senses, this might be a case of separately derived homophones, or a case where separate partially-similar terms influenced the meaning.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Listed as borrowed from French nuance or English nuance.
Some Japanese sources do not indicate a source language and only list the etymon form, as nuance, which is the format in these works to indicate an origin from English. Other references explicitly list both French and English as source languages, or just French.
First cited to ふらんす物語 (Furansu Monogatari), a 1909 book by 永井荷風 (Nagai Kafū).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The instrument derives from the Okinawan 三線 (sanshin). Originally called 蛇皮線 (jabisen, literally “snakeskin strings”) in Japanese, so named for the way the Okinawan instrument's soundbox is traditionally covered in snakeskin. The traditional jabisen instrument was imported into the Sakai area of Osaka during the Eiroku era (1558–1570), then later modified by biwa luthiers to have the square-shaped shamisen soundbox of today.
The reading jabisen shifted over time to 蛇味線 (jamisen), replacing the 皮 (bi, “skin, leather”) character with 味 (mi) for phonetic reasons, i.e. as ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Then jamisen changed to shamisen, replacing the 蛇 (ja, “snake”) character with 三 (sha , usually read san, “three”) for semantic reasons. The sha reading for the 三 character is irregular.
The shamisen reading is first cited to a text from 1580.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Sound shift from shamisen above, possibly influenced by the standard san reading of the initial 三 character.
This reading appears to be less common than shamisen.
First cited to a text from 1632.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally from Middle Chinese 乙 (MC 'it), arising from the proper noun sense. Appears in texts from at least 833 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By extension from the moving tone noun sense. Appears in texts from the late Edo period, in the early 1800s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived as aggressive clipping of お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu, used as a kind of greeting at work, literally “that's honorable exhaustion (from hard work)”). The use of 乙 for the spelling is an example of phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 木 (Ki, “Wood”, one of the Five Elements) + の (no, attributive marker) + 弟 (oto, “younger brother”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Cognate with the initial oto- in 劣る (otoru, “to be less than; to be younger than”), 落とす (otosu, “to drop something”). Also the first element in 弟 (otōto, “younger brother”).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712.
This is distinct from the initial oto- in 乙女(おとめ) (otome), which can instead be traced to an earlier woto- root, cognate with 復(を)つ (wotu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 代(だい) (dai-, “substitute, in substitution for someone else”) + 弁(べん) (ben, “speech”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 光熱(こうねつ) (kōnetsu, “lighting and heating”) + 費(ひ) (-hi, “expense”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 免る (manukaru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from 目(ま) (ma-, “eye”) + 抜(ぬ)かる (nukaru, “to mistake”).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 切 (setsu, "keen," "acute," "intense") + 実 (jitsu, "faithfulness," "sincerity," "fidelity").

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 墓地 (muᴴ dijᴴ, literally “grave, tomb + ground, region”). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin reading mùdì, Min Nan bōng-tē.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 墓 (haka, “grave”, from Old Japanese) + 地 (chi, “ground, region”, from Middle Chinese).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 増(ま)す (masu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 家(いえ) (ie, “house”) + 出(で) (de, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 出(で)る (deru, “to go out, exit”))

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First cited in the Man'yōshū of 759.
Derived as the regular classical causative conjugation of 悩む (nayamu, “to be vexed”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 感(かん) (kan, “emotion”) + 無量(むりょう) (muryō, “immeasurable”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, as the long form of 我 (wa) below.
Compound of 我 (wa, see below) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 我 (wa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 打ち (uchi, verbal prefix adding euphony or emphasis) + 切る (kiru, “terminate an action”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 最(さい) (sai-, “most”) + 善(ぜん) (zen, “good”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Root of the Old Japanese verb ぬる (nuru, “to become loose; to become wet”) and modern Japanese 濡れる (nureru, “to become wet”), adverb ぬるぬる (nurunuru, “loosely; lukewarmly; oozingly”).
May be cognate with Korean 늪 (neup, “swamp, bog, marsh”), Ainu nup (“flat land, plain; fen”), Mongolian нам (nam, “low-lying”), намаг (namag, “swamp, bog, marsh”), норох (norox, “to become wet”).
Generally only used in compounds in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be a compound of 沼 (nu, “swamp”) + 間 (ma, “space, area”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/seu/ → /ɕeu/ → /ɕʲoː/
From Middle Chinese 沼 (tsyew^X, “swamp”). Compare modern Mandarin 沼 (zhǎo).
Only ever used in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 無(む) (mu-, “un-”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “mouth”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literally "thing of hair". Compound of 毛 (ke, “hair”) + だ (da, genitive marker) + 物 (mono, “thing”). Medial -da- is a very rare genitive marker found in compounds, also seen in 果物 (kudamono, “fruit”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literally "hair thing". Compound of 毛 (ke, “hair”) + 物 (mono, “thing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *sisi. Cognate with 肉 (shishi, “meat of a beast”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/siu/ → /ɕiu/ → /d͡ʑiu/ → /d͡ʑuː/
From Middle Chinese 獸 /兽 (syuwᴴ, “(wild) animal”). Compare modern Mandarin reading shòu, Min Nan siù.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 緩(ゆる)い (yurui, “loose”) + む (mu, “-ize, -en”, verbal suffix).
Occasionally pronounced with a medial /b/ as 緩(ゆる)ぶ (yurubu), especially historically. Copmpare similar alternation of /m/ and /b/ seen in 寒い (sabui, samui), 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 膨る (pukuru), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”), from Proto-Japonic *pukoru.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Compare 膨らむ (fukuramu, “to swell, to get bigger”), 膨らます (fukuramasu, “to make swell, to fill up”), and 袋 (fukuro, “bag”), from the way a bag is filled with items.
First cited to the Man’yōshū, completed sometime after 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from 藝.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 藝 /艺 (ngjiejᴴ, “art, skill”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally derived from 蕓 into a separate character; not a shinjitai form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from verb 重(おも)んずる (omonzuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 雜 (MC dzop).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
From stem kasu-, cognate with its active counterpart 霞(かす)める (kasumeru, “to blur, to obscure”), adjective かすか (kasuka, “faint, dim”, and its classical form 幽(かすけ)し (kasukeshi)), adverb かすかす (kasukasu, “barely”), verb 掠(かす)める (kasumeru, “to rob; to sweep over”),, and verbs 擦(かす)る (kasuru, “to graze, to touch lightly”) and かすれる (kasureru, “to graze; to be blurred; to be hoarse”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with 霞(かす)む (kasumu, “to grow hazy, to become blurry”) above.
